summary: Defines a protocol for fetching cryptographic credentials from a credential server using a workstation with trusted software but no personal setup. Payloads are XML, with a BEEP profile, and TLS or DIGEST-MD5 security is required. It was updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: You sit at any computer, ask a safe server for your keys, and it gives them. This is the language for that request.

questions: how to get private keys from a credential server
how does sacred protect against dictionary attacks
subtitle: A protocol for fetching your private keys and certificates from a credential server using any trusted workstation.

tldr.problem: Users want to use the same private keys and certificates on different devices, but import and export tools are impractical on a desktop and may not exist at all on constrained or wireless devices.
tldr.mechanism: A client authenticates to a credential server with a username and password and uploads, downloads or deletes named credentials, using XML messages carried in a BEEP profile protected by TLS and DIGEST-MD5.
tldr.outcome: The protocol is designed so that eavesdropping or impersonation gives an attacker nothing to start a dictionary attack with. It is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3767 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 8996; no RFC obsoletes it according to the unit metadata. Check that update for changes to the TLS requirements before relying on the text above.

sections.title: Fetching Credentials from a Server
sections.content:
Digital credentials, such as private keys and their certificates, support protocols like S/MIME, IPSec and TLS. Users often want the same credentials on several devices, but moving them by hand is impractical and some devices lack the tools. SACRED (Securely Available Credentials) is a protocol for the secure exchange of such credentials, and a realization of the framework in RFC 3760. It meets the requirements of RFC 3157.

The design assumes the only authentication information the user has is a username and password. Many user-chosen passwords are vulnerable to dictionary attacks, so the protocol aims to give an attacker nothing to launch one with, whether by eavesdropping or by impersonating the client or the server.

Two passwords may be involved: the account password authenticates the user to the credential server, and the credential password decrypts parts of a credential after download. The RFC says this approach is somewhat less secure than a smart card, but it is useful until smart cards are common and as a backup when a card is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Your keys live in a safe at a trusted bank. At any computer you can ask the bank for them, if you can prove who you are with a password.

sections.title: Account Management Operations
sections.content:
Four account operations are optional for both servers and clients. The Information Request needs no authentication: the client sends an empty InfoRequest and the server answers with an InfoResponse listing its authentication parameters (for DIGEST-MD5, at least one realm) and the ProcessInfo types it supports.

Create Account requires server authentication. The client sends a CreateAccountRequest with the account name and, for DIGEST-MD5, a password verifier (the hashed username, password and realm) and the chosen realm. Remove Account requires mutual authentication, and the server MUST delete all information about the account. Modify Account also requires mutual authentication and lets the client change its authentication information, such as a realm and a password verifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can use the safe you have to open an account, and you can also close the account or change your password. Looking at the bank's rules needs no ID at all.

sections.title: Upload, Download and Delete
sections.content:
The run-time operations MUST be supported by every conformant implementation, and all require mutual authentication. A DownloadRequest may carry a credential selector string; no selector, or an empty one, means all credentials for the account. The server replies with a DownloadResponse containing one or more credentials, each with a LastModified time set by the server.

An UploadRequest MUST contain one credential. A credential with the same selector is replaced; otherwise a new one is added. The LastModified value sent in the upload MUST be the one most recently received in a download, and this lets the server spot conflicts, for example when two platforms download and then both update. In that case the server MUST respond with a BEEP error, which SHOULD be StaleCredential. The server overwrites the value with its own current time when it stores the credential.

A DeleteRequest contains either a CredentialSelector or an All element. If a selector is given with a LastModified value that does not match, the server MUST NOT delete the credential. If no matching credential exists, the server returns an error.
sections.plainLanguage: You can take your keys out, put new keys in, or throw them away. The server stamps a time on each key, so if two people change the same key, it notices the mix-up.

sections.title: Required Session Security
sections.content:
Every operation except the Information Request needs confidentiality and integrity, plus either server authentication (Create Account) or mutual authentication (everything else). Credential servers are REQUIRED to support TLS and DIGEST-MD5, and clients MUST support DIGEST-MD5 and TLS with server authentication.

The mandatory-to-implement TLS cipher suite is TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES-EDE_CBC_SHA, and implementations SHOULD also support TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. For client authentication, DIGEST-MD5 MUST only be used inside a TLS server-authenticated pipe, and only for authenticating the client; its own confidentiality and integrity services are not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The conversation happens inside a sealed tube, and only after the tube is sealed do you show your password, so nobody can peek.

sections.title: Credentials and Selectors
sections.content:
A Credential element has these fields: a CredentialSelector that names it within the account; a PayLoad holding a ds:KeyInfo or another credential form, where implementations MUST support the PKCS #15 form (the SacredPKCS15 element); LastModified, the server time of the last change; an optional TimeToLive hint, in seconds, that clients SHOULD honor; and optional ProcessInfo and ClientInfo extension fields.

There is no concept of a default credential. Every credential MUST have a selector that is unique in the account, required for uploads and optional for downloads. ProcessInfo data is for the server to process, for example a phone number the server demands, while ClientInfo is for the client and the server MUST ignore it. Clients may store a signature over the credential in ClientInfo and check it before using the private key.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key goes in a labelled envelope. The label has to be different for every envelope, so you can ask for just the one you need or for all of them.

sections.title: The BEEP Profile and Errors
sections.content:
The messages are XML, with a schema in Appendix A, and are carried in a BEEP profile (see RFC 3080) identified as http://iana.org/beep/sacred. Because nearly every operation has security requirements, the BEEP session will likely first be tuned with TLS, or with TLS followed by DIGEST-MD5. Messages are exchanged as application/beep+xml, and each request has a matching reply: InfoRequest gets InfoResponse, DownloadRequest gets DownloadResponse, and the others get ok, or any of them an error.

Errors use standard BEEP reply codes such as 421, 450, 451, 454, 500, 501, 504, 530, 534, 535, 537, 538, 550, 553 and 554. Three SACRED-specific codes are added. Appendix C notes that SACRED may run in a non-BEEP environment if the application protocol is protected according to the security mandates first.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages ride on a delivery system called BEEP, which already knows how to lock the doors first. If something goes wrong, the server answers with a numbered error.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC walks through twelve vulnerabilities listed in the requirements document (V1 to V12). Passive eavesdropping and online impersonation of the server are countered by DIGEST-MD5 and TLS and by server or mutual authentication. Attacks on the repository are met with a SHOULD that server implementations protect the database, and servers MAY add protection against online dictionary attacks on accounts. For denial of service, no specific countermeasures are proposed in the table, though servers SHOULD drop inactive connections and minimize resources for unauthenticated ones.

If the server database is stolen, an attacker can run a dictionary attack, and if it succeeds can decrypt the user's credentials and upload new ones. Clients SHOULD check the TLS server using the checks in section 3.1 of RFC 2818 and include the BEEP serverName in the start message, otherwise a spoof server could gain access to a user's credential. A man-in-the-middle attack is thwarted by the DIGEST-MD5 digest-uri-value, which for SACRED is sacred/<serverName>.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the ways a thief might try to trick you and says how each is blocked. The biggest risk is the server's own storage being stolen, so it must be guarded well.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has registered the BEEP profile http://iana.org/beep/sacred. The SACRED protocol SHOULD be run over port 1118, and the GSSAPI service name that is required when using SASL SHALL be sacred.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol gets its own official name and a suggested door number, 1118, so everyone knows where to knock.
